prompt:
The patient recently returned from international travel, spending about 10 days in rural areas of Asia and, several months later, about 10 days in rural areas of South America. They have never had active GI symptoms but were told to consider post-exposure anti-helminth and anti-protozoal treatment. Is there any benefit to anti-helminth or anti-protozoal treatment in an otherwise asymptomatic patient, and does any testing need to be done first?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Obtain a detailed itinerary and exposure history, including specific destinations, freshwater contact, barefoot soil exposure, sanitation, food and water sources, insect exposure, and animal contact.
Assess for current or prior fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, rash, pruritus, cough, or hematuria.
Review pregnancy status, immunosuppression, planned corticosteroid therapy, and medication contraindications before considering antiparasitic treatment.
Counsel that empiric anti-helminthic or anti-protozoal therapy is not routinely recommended for an asymptomatic short-term traveler without a specific high-risk exposure or positive test.
Obtain a CBC with differential when the exposure history raises concern for helminth infection or eosinophilia.
Order Strongyloides stercoralis IgG serology when there was meaningful endemic soil exposure, unexplained eosinophilia, or anticipated immunosuppression.
Order Schistosoma IgG serology after an appropriate post-exposure interval when freshwater exposure occurred in an endemic area.
Order targeted stool ova and parasite examinations if compatible gastrointestinal symptoms or otherwise unexplained eosinophilia develops.
Order Giardia and Cryptosporidium stool antigen or PCR testing if persistent diarrhea develops.
Order Entamoeba histolytica stool antigen or PCR testing if dysentery or colitis symptoms develop.
Schedule follow-up to review any targeted test results and reassess for new symptoms.
Counsel the patient to seek reevaluation for diarrhea, fever, abdominal pain, weight loss, rash, hematuria, pruritus, or cough.
Advise urgent evaluation for fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area.
Refer to infectious disease or travel medicine when testing is abnormal, exposure risk is substantial, or interpretation is uncertain.
Treat confirmed uncomplicated Strongyloides infection with ivermectin 200 mcg/kg orally daily for 1 to 2 days.
Treat confirmed schistosomiasis with an appropriate species-specific praziquantel regimen.
Treat a confirmed soil-transmitted helminth infection with the recommended organism-specific anti-helminthic regimen.

Treat confirmed Giardia infection with a recommended regimen when symptoms or a specific transmission-risk indication warrants treatment, explaining that otherwise asymptomatic infection does not routinely require medication.
Treat confirmed invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection with a tissue-active nitroimidazole.
Give a luminal amebicide after tissue-active treatment for confirmed invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection.
Repeat Strongyloides serology after an appropriate interval if the initial test was obtained too early after a confirmed high-risk exposure.
Prescribe empiric albendazole without a documented indication or diagnostic evidence of helminth infection.
Prescribe empiric ivermectin without a targeted indication or diagnostic evidence of Strongyloides infection.
Prescribe empiric praziquantel without endemic freshwater exposure or evidence of schistosomiasis.
Prescribe empiric metronidazole, tinidazole, or nitazoxanide for broad protozoal coverage in an asymptomatic traveler.
Prescribe an empiric multidrug anti-helminthic regimen without diagnostic evidence or a specific high-risk exposure.

Initiate empiric antimalarial treatment or new post-exposure chemoprophylaxis in an asymptomatic returned traveler without a specific indication (as distinct from completing an existing prophylaxis regimen or indicated terminal prophylaxis).
Order routine or repeated stool ova and parasite examinations, stool protozoal stains, stool antigen tests, or multiplex gastrointestinal PCR in a low-risk asymptomatic traveler.
Order a broad untargeted parasitic serology panel without an exposure-specific indication.
Order Strongyloides serology in an asymptomatic patient without endemic exposure, eosinophilia, or anticipated immunosuppression.
Order Schistosoma serology in an asymptomatic patient without freshwater exposure in an endemic region.
Order Entamoeba histolytica serology solely because of travel to an endemic region.
Order Toxoplasma IgM or IgG serology without a specific clinical indication.
Order malaria rapid testing or blood smears in an entirely asymptomatic traveler.
Order abdominal imaging or brain imaging solely to screen an asymptomatic traveler for parasitic infection.
Perform endoscopy or colonoscopy solely to search for parasites in an asymptomatic traveler.
Perform liver biopsy without imaging, laboratory, or serologic evidence of parasitic liver involvement.
Refer solely to obtain empiric deworming despite the absence of symptoms, abnormal testing, or a high-risk exposure.
Tell the patient that empiric antiparasitic treatment is harmless and routinely recommended after tropical travel.
Tell the patient that no future evaluation is needed even if compatible symptoms develop.
